strengths: Well-motivated core idea with clear intuition that language can resolve monocular depth ambiguities through geometric priors learned in text-to-image pre-training
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across four benchmarks with extensive ablation studies (prompts, templates, denoising steps) and qualitative visualizations
Demonstrates multiple beneficial properties: faster training convergence (20K vs 30K iterations), fewer inference steps (10 vs 25), and improved small object perception
Practical robustness shown through template prompt experiments (Table 5) when detailed descriptions unavailable, demonstrating real-world applicability
Thorough implementation details and well-organized presentation with effective visualizations of improvements
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: straightforward addition of CLIP text encoder to Marigold without architectural innovations or diffusion-specific advances

Circular reasoning about 'language prior': descriptions generated by LLaVA (vision-language model) are derived from visual information, undermining claims of independent language priors and less covariate shift
Marginal final performance improvements over baseline (typically <1% on δ1 and AbsRel metrics across benchmarks, within measurement noise)
Heavy dependence on expensive LLaVA preprocessing (740K captions, 740 GPU hours) with no analysis of caption quality, diversity, or per-image variation; severely limits reproducibility
Missing comparisons with other language-based depth methods (WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) despite citing them; only compares against image-only Marigold baseline
Weak mechanistic explanation for convergence speedup: claims about learning from 'low-dimensional language features' lack quantitative validation and rigorous investigation
Limited failure case analysis (single example in Figure 9) without systematic study of when/how incorrect descriptions degrade performance
Overstated claims (e.g., 'state-of-the-art') when improvements are marginal and not positioned against other language-based methods

strengths: Clear motivation for using language to resolve monocular depth ambiguities
Comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across four benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet)
Extensive qualitative visualizations showing improvements on small and occluded objects
Supplementary material includes multiple ablations (prompts, templates, denoising steps)
Demonstrates faster training convergence (20K vs 30K iterations vs Marigold)
weaknesses: Minimal technical novelty—trivial application of existing diffusion models with straightforward text conditioning
Critical flaw: Claims to leverage human language priors but uses auto-generated LLaVA descriptions, introducing confounding variables and undermining core premise
Marginal quantitative improvements that are inconsistent across datasets (< 1% in most metrics) and potentially within noise
No proper ablation of language contribution; Table 5 shows method works with blank text/generic templates (95.7 vs 96.0 δ1), contradicting the claim that meaningful language helps
Missing direct comparisons with other language-based depth methods (WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) despite citing them; only compares to Marigold
Misleading claims of 'state-of-the-art performance'—Depth Anything v2 substantially outperforms (97.9 vs 96.0 δ1 on NYUv2, 94.8 vs 90.6 on KITTI)
Small area improvements (Table 2) only evaluated on NYUv2 and still marginal (~1.2%); small regions detected from images, not from language descriptions
Auto-generated descriptions confound results—LLaVA re-encodes visual information, making it unclear if improvements come from language or additional visual processing
No analysis of which linguistic features actually drive depth improvements; no attention visualizations or feature analysis
Convergence speed claims are misleading; faster training with language conditioning doesn't validate better depth quality when final performance is comparable
Practical applicability undermined by method working with template prompts, suggesting language content is not critical
No ablation removing language entirely to quantify its actual contribution to depth estimation
Computational overhead of caption generation (740 GPU hours) not addressed or compared
Single run results without error bars or multiple seeds; differences < 1% lack statistical rigor
Trained on only 74K synthetic images with zero-shot evaluation only; no evaluation on diverse out-of-distribution scenarios

strengths: Novel application of language priors from text-to-image diffusion models to monocular depth estimation with clear, well-motivated intuition
Impressive data efficiency: achieves state-of-the-art zero-shot performance on four datasets using only 74K training images, competitive with methods trained on 62.6M+ images
Significant efficiency improvements: faster training convergence (20k vs 30k iterations) and fewer inference steps required (10 vs 25 steps), providing practical benefits
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with thorough ablation studies on prompt design, analysis of small object performance, and detailed supplementary material
Well-written paper with clear presentation, informative visualizations, and reproducible experimental setup following proper zero-shot evaluation protocol
Demonstrates controllable depth estimation capability where appending language details progressively improves predictions for specified regions
weaknesses: Critical dependency on text description quality with limited robustness analysis; Figure 9 failure case shows incorrect descriptions mislead the model, but no systematic analysis of error types or frequency

Modest absolute performance improvements when compared to Marigold at same training iterations; at 30k iterations many differences narrow significantly, suggesting convergence speed is main advantage rather than superior final performance

Substantial computational overhead for generating descriptions (740 GPU hours to create 740,000 captions), plus dependency on LLaVA v1.6 which may become unavailable; undermines 'language prior' claim when descriptions are auto-generated rather than human-provided
Limited technical novelty; architecture is straightforward adaptation of Marigold with frozen CLIP text encoder, using only standard components from existing models

Incomplete analysis of language contribution: missing attention visualizations, no investigation of which description aspects are most useful, no ablation of training with language vs testing without it

Synthetic-to-real domain gap addressed only through prompt workaround ('real-world image'); no systematic analysis of transfer quality or comparison of description patterns between synthetic and real domains
Missing comparisons to other language-based depth methods (DepthCLIP, WorDepth, RSA) mentioned in related work despite being most relevant baselines
Limited failure analysis with only one example shown; no systematic characterization of failure modes, problem frequencies, or types of scenes/objects where method struggles most
Underdeveloped controllability claims; Figure 6 shows progressive improvement but lacks formal evaluation and no user studies validating 'user intent' guidance claims

strengths: Well-motivated core insight: language provides semantic and geometric constraints to resolve monocular depth ambiguities (texture ambiguity, visibility ambiguity, small object perception)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: tests on 3 diffusion models (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) across 5 diverse real-world datasets with consistent improvements
Extensive supplementary analysis: thorough ablations on prompt design, caption counts, denoising steps, template prompts, and convergence behavior

Interesting secondary findings: convergence speedup (10 vs 25 steps), better small object perception, iterative refinement capability, and surprising benefits when text provided only at training or inference
Clear presentation with effective qualitative visualizations demonstrating improvements in specified regions, especially for small/occluded objects
weaknesses: Marginal quantitative improvements without statistical significance testing: δ1 gains typically <0.5%, AbsRel <0.3%; many results show minimal change or regression (e.g., Lotus-G on ETH3D)

Critical evaluation methodology flaw: evaluation entirely uses automatically generated text descriptions (LLaVA/InternVL) rather than human annotations, creating potential circular dependency and preventing assessment of true upper bounds
No comparison with related language-enhanced depth methods (WorDepth, RSA) or other language-integrated approaches (DepthCLIP) cited in related work, making it impossible to assess relative merits
Limited technical novelty: straightforward concatenation of CLIP text encoding with image features in standard conditional diffusion framework; no architectural innovations
Inconsistent results across models and datasets (performance sometimes degrades, especially for Lotus-G) without analysis of why method is dataset-dependent, raising concerns about generalization
Significant practical limitations: dependency on external VLM inference for text generation (740 GPU hours for training captions), no computational cost analysis, code not available

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: explanations for why text helps at training-only or inference-only time are speculative; lacks analysis of what geometric/semantic information is actually captured

Zero-shot evaluation only on synthetic-trained models; no fine-tuning experiments on real data; evaluation limited to standard benchmarks without challenging scenarios (extreme occlusion, motion blur)

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 3 base models and 5 datasets with extensive ablation studies on prompts, denoising steps, and caption numbers
Clear evidence of faster diffusion convergence with language conditioning (10 vs 25 steps in Table 4)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations including failure cases with incorrect text (Figure 9)
Focused improvements demonstrated for small objects and text-described regions (Table 2, Figures 4-5)
Thorough implementation details and commitment to code release support reproducibility
weaknesses: Marginal quantitative improvements without statistical significance testing: Marigold NYUv2 δ1 only improves 0.2 pp (95.7→95.9), KITTI 0.9 pp (89.7→90.6); no error bars or confidence intervals provided despite small effect sizes

Fundamental methodological flaw: uses automatically generated text from VLMs (LLaVA, InternVL3) that see the same images, creating circular reasoning—unclear if improvements come from semantic language understanding or just auxiliary supervision from automatic descriptions

Missing direct comparisons with existing language-based depth methods (DepthCLIP [83], WordDepth [76], RSA [77]); Table 1 only compares against vision-only baselines, making it impossible to assess relative performance

Inconsistent results undermine core claims: Table 1 shows training-only or inference-only text sometimes outperforms both, with limited explanation; unclear mechanistic understanding of when/why language helps

Impractical applicability: requires accurate text descriptions at inference time; circular dependency where quality of descriptions depends on visual recognition (same problem depth estimation faces); no evaluation of robustness to description quality
Minimal technical novelty: straightforward application of freezing CLIP encoder and concatenating features; no architectural innovations or depth-aware text processing mechanisms

Limited practical impact: improvements of ~0.2-0.9 pp on standard metrics at high computational cost (740 GPU hours for caption generation; 3.6s per image at inference); convergence speed improvement doesn't proportionally improve final accuracy

Insufficient experimental rigor: no human-annotated text experiments to validate whether improvements require semantic language; different VLMs used for different models (LLaVA vs InternVL3) without justification; no ablation on text encoder choice

Vague technical details on text integration: unclear where text features are concatenated in network; how feature dimensions are matched; why token limit of 77 tokens; no cross-attention vs concatenation comparison

Text generation bias not addressed: automatic descriptions may be biased toward easily detectable visual features; no comparison between human-written vs LLaVA-generated text; different prompts (Table 3) show varying results but claimed as 'consistently comparable'

strengths: Clear and well-motivated hypothesis connecting text-to-image pre-training to depth estimation, with excellent intuitive explanations
Comprehensive evaluation across three baseline models (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) and five real-world datasets (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet, DIODE)
Consistent improvements across settings, including valuable findings about faster convergence (Figure 7), reduced denoising steps (10 vs 25), and better small-area performance (Table 2)
Thorough ablation studies in supplementary material covering prompts, caption counts, denoising steps, and template prompts, supporting reproducibility
Well-presented paper with clear figures and intuitive visualizations effectively demonstrating improvements in ambiguous/small regions
Demonstrates iterative refinement capability with progressively detailed text descriptions (Figure 6)
Pragmatic use of vision-language models (LLaVA, InternVL3) to generate descriptions, addressing annotation scarcity
weaknesses: Quantitative improvements are modest and often inconsistent: improvements of 0.2-0.3 in δ₁ metrics (Table 1), with some models showing degradation (E2E-FT AbsRel: 5.4→6.2); no statistical significance testing or error bars provided
Critical missing comparisons with directly related language-based methods: WorDepth [76] and RSA [77] are cited but not experimentally compared—a significant gap for a language-guided depth paper

Heavy dependence on automatically generated text descriptions; Figure 9 demonstrates clear failure modes with incorrect text; no systematic robustness analysis for text quality, length, or specificity variations

Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward concatenation of CLIP embeddings with visual features; no investigation of architectural choices (frozen vs. fine-tuned encoder, attention mechanisms, etc.)

Computational overhead inadequately addressed: text generation requires 740 GPU hours; no analysis of runtime/memory costs during training/inference or cost-benefit tradeoffs relative to 0.2-point improvements
Unclear mechanism: no attention visualizations, gradient analysis, or investigation of how text information is actually used; explanations for training/inference-only improvements remain speculative
Inconsistent results across models (Lotus-D degrades from 97.2→96.8 in δ₁; E2E-FT shows worse AbsRel), raising questions about generalization and when language helps
Different vision-language models used for different baselines (LLaVA vs. InternVL3), complicating fair comparison and reproducibility
Limited analysis of when/why language helps: only demonstrated for small areas; no systematic evaluation across scene types, lighting, occlusion patterns, or real-world conditions
